name: Bone-extending procedures
lead: Bone-extending procedures are surgeries that lengthen the legs (and occasionally other bones) to add height. The surgeon cuts the bone and slowly separates the pieces so new bone forms in the gap, a method known as distraction osteogenesis.[1] People pursue it to gain stature and, in some cases, to correct leg shape or proportion.[2]

The technique grew out of work by Gavriil Ilizarov, who developed external fixators and distraction rates from the 1950s and 1960s.[1][2] The first reported cosmetic case, in Volgograd in 1992, lengthened a healthy patient's tibia by 6 cm over 11 months.[2] Modern options include external frames and fully implantable motorized nails such as the Fitbone.[1]

chain: Bone is cut and gradually distracted
New bone fills the gap over months
Permanently longer legs and added height
angle.text: Surgeons lengthen the tibia or femur by gradual distraction, producing a permanent gain of several centimetres in stature; the first cosmetic case added 6 cm. It is the route people choose when they want durable added height.

infobox: 17 and older, after growth plates close[2]

paras: The phases are osteotomy (cutting the bone), a latency period of about a week, distraction at roughly 1 mm per day, and consolidation while the new bone hardens, with hardware removed in a later operation for some systems.[1] Indications listed for cosmetic lengthening include legs short relative to body height, bowing, and distress about height.[2]

Bernhard von Langenbeck proposed the idea in 1869 and Alessandro Codivilla published the first clinical attempt in 1905, with high complication rates.[1] Ilizarov's studies of many patients from the 1950s defined workable distraction rates and fixators, making the method widespread.[1] Cosmetic use in healthy patients began in Russia in 1992.[2]

No studies found on cosmetic height surgery specifically in the sources reviewed here. Studies of limb lengthening for deformity report infection in about 5% overall, bone failing to grow as intended in roughly 7 to 9%, and hardware failure in roughly 3 to 4.5%.[1]

Reported complications include infection, nonunion if distraction is too fast, hardware failure, nerve injury and further operations.[1] In India, where cosmetic lengthening is in demand and unregulated, some patients reported infections and extra surgeries, and China banned limb lengthening in 2006 after operations with serious side effects.[1]

Height surgery is discussed as the permanent option among height-increase methods, with attention to cost, recovery time and surgeon choice. In India, height is described as valued for marriage and career prospects.[1]

timeline.event: Ilizarov develops external fixation and distraction rates.[1]
First cosmetic lengthening of a healthy patient, Volgograd.[2]

card.summary: Surgery that gradually lengthens leg bones to add permanent height.
card.aka: Limb lengthening, height surgery, leg lengthening
card.note: Major surgery with months of recovery and a recognised complication rate.

quick.overview:
Bone-extending procedures cut a leg bone and slowly pull the ends apart so new bone grows in between. The result is permanent added height, historically several centimetres per bone.

The first cosmetic case in 1992 added 6 cm to a tibia over 11 months.
quick.mechanism: Distraction osteogenesis: osteotomy, a short wait, lengthening of about 1 mm per day with an external frame or motorized nail, then months of bone consolidation.
quick.risks: Reported complications include infection (about 5%), poor bone healing, hardware failure and nerve injury. Regulation varies; China banned the procedure in 2006.
